channel.description: Debezium is an open source distributed platform for change data capture. Start it up, point it at your databases, and your apps can start responding to all of the inserts, updates, and deletes that other apps commit to your databases. Debezium is durable and fast, so your apps can respond quickly and never miss an event, even when things go wrong.

item.title: Debezium Joins Google Summer of Code 2026!
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Panice
item.description:
We’re thrilled to announce that Debezium is participating in Google Summer of Code (GSoC) for 2026! 🎉

As part of the JBoss Community’s GSoC organization, Debezium is offering several projects for contributors to work with change data capture (CDC), vector database technologies, Quarkus, and artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML). These are all aimed at expanding the Debezium ecosystem.

GSoC is a fantastic opportunity for aspiring contributors to gain hands‑on engineering experience while being mentored by open-source maintainers. If you’re passionate about distributed systems, data streaming, and CDC, this is the perfect opportunity to dive in.

🚀 Debezium Project Ideas for GSoC 2026

Below are the Debezium‑related projects available for this year’s program, as listed on the official Jboss Community GSoC ideas page:

  1. Debezium Source Connector for Milvus: implement a new source connector to capture changes from Milvus, the popular vector database.

  2. Debezium Source Connector for SQLite implement a new source connector to capture changes from SQLite, one of the most widely used embedded databases.

  3. Debezium CLI: a dedicated command-line interface for making setup, debugging, and deployment more intuitive.

  4. Host-Based Pipeline Deployment for the Debezium Platform: enhance Debezium’s platform-level capabilities by improving the deployment.

  5. PyDebeziumAI: explore how AI can enhance Debezium via Python

💬 Upcoming AMA Session for Contributors

To help interested candidates get familiar with the projects, mentors, and expectations, we’ll be hosting an Ask-Me-Anything (AMA) session. After the session, candidates should be well-equipped to begin discussing ideas with their mentors.

📅 Date: 5th March 2026 2.30PM CET

🎬Platform: youtube.com

🎙️ Who should attend? Anyone considering applying for one of the Debezium projects.

🤝 How to Get Started

  • Read through the full GSoC 2026 idea list for the JBoss Community.

  • Join the discussion official channels for Jboss Community.

  • Join the Debezium Zulip Chat and subscribe to the community-gsoc channel

  • Follow Debezium on linkedin for updates

  • Read the contribution guidelines

  • Familiarize yourself with Debezium by taking a good-first-issue

We’re excited to welcome the next generation of contributors to the Debezium community. Stay tuned for more details and get ready for an incredible GSoC season!

item.title: Introducing reusable Connections in the Debezium Platform
item.dc:creator: Indra Raj Shukla
item.description:
The Debezium Platform aims to simplify the building and management of CDC data pipelines by streamlining infrastructure setup.

Earlier, connection-related properties (such as hostnames, ports, credentials, and authentication details) were defined directly in the Source or Destination configuration. While this worked, it often led to duplication and harder maintenance of the same connection details across multiple instances.

To address this, we are introducing Connections as a first-class citizen in the Debezium Platform, making it easier for you to manage connection details in one place and avoid repetitive setup.

Connections allow you to define, validate, and reuse connection details independently, reducing configuration errors and saving time by referencing them in multiple Sources and Destinations.

What are Connections?

A Connection specifies the configuration required to connect to an external system, like a source database or a sink endpoint.

Instead of embedding these details inside each Source or Destination:

  • You create a Connection once

  • Validate it independently

  • Reuse it across multiple Sources and Destinations

This makes pipelines easier to manage, safer to modify, and faster to set up.

Why introduce Connections?

Rather than defining connection details inside each Source or Destination, separating them as a first-class citizen provides a host of benefits:

Reusability

A single Connection can be reused across multiple Sources or Destinations.

Centralized management

Update credentials or connection parameters in one place without editing every pipeline.

Early validation

Validate a Connection before it is ever used by a Source or Destination.

Cleaner configurations

Source and Destination definitions focus only on CDC and data-flow logic, not on infrastructure details.

All these benefits make creating and managing pipelines easier, safer, and faster.

Creating a Connection

You can create a Connection directly from the catalog or during the resource creation flow.

Connection catalog.

When creating a Connection, you define the connection-specific properties required to communicate with the external system (for example, database host, port, authentication details, or sink endpoint configuration).

Once defined, the Connection can be validated independently to ensure it is correctly configured and reachable.

Validating a Connection

A key part of the new Connection workflow is connection validation.

Connection validation and creation.

After creating a Connection, you can explicitly validate it to verify that:

  • The configuration is complete

  • The platform can successfully connect to the target system

  • Authentication and network settings are correct

This helps catch issues early, before a Source or Destination is created or a pipeline is started.

Using Connections in Sources and Destinations

When defining a Source or Destination, all validated Connection definitions are available in a drop-down for quick access, making pipeline setup and management fast and straightforward.

Select connection for source

This allows the same Connection to be shared across:

  • Multiple Sources or Destination

  • Multiple pipelines

Updating existing workflows

If you know how to create Sources and Destinations in Debezium, the workflow is unchanged, and updating to use Connection definitions is quick and painless.

First, create a Connection definition with all the connection properties your existing pipeline uses. After you create and validate the Connection, simply edit the workflow and select the newly defined Connection definition to link it to the pipeline. The pipeline then uses the reusable Connection definition moving forward.

Demo: Connections in action

More coming soon!

Connections lay the foundation for making the Debezium Platform more modular, maintainable, and scalable.

We’ll continue to build on this with further improvements and new features in upcoming releases.

As always, feel free to leave a comment below or get in touch with us on the mailing list or in our Zulip chat.

item.title: LLMs in the Loop: Using AI to Migrate JUnit Tests
item.dc:creator: Fiore Mario Vitale
item.description:
JUnit 5 was released in late 2017, and since then the migration from JUnit 4 has been written about extensively, so much so that, at first glance, it may feel like an old and well-trodden topic.

JUnit usage statistics

Yet in reality, the chart makes it clear that JUnit 4 is still very much alive in the ecosystem. According to Libraries.io, JUnit 4 has 91.5K dependent packages and 29.3K dependent repositories. By comparison, JUnit 5’s junit-jupiter-engine has only 20.8K dependent packages and 5.3K dependent repositories.

Clearly, there are still many projects running on JUnit 4 today.

item.title: Tracking Debezium issues on GitHub
item.dc:creator: Jiri Pechanec
item.description:
Introduction

As part of Debezium’s transition to the Commonhaus Foundation, we are also evolving how we track issues and plan work.

Until now, the Debezium project has relied on the Red Hat Jira instance as the primary place to report bugs, request enhancements, and track larger initiatives. Over time, however, our day-to-day development has increasingly centered around GitHub, with pull requests, discussions, and automation already happening there.

To align with this new governance model and simplify the contribution experience, we are moving Debezium issue tracking from Red Hat Jira to GitHub Issues.

What is changing

Starting in December 2025, the Debezium team will use GitHub Issues as the canonical place to track bugs, feature requests, and other work items for the project.

More concretely:

  • New issues will be reported using GitHub Issues in the relevant Debezium repository.

  • The existing Debezium Jira project (DBZ) will be retired and moved to read-only mode.

  • Open issues from Jira will be copied into GitHub Issues so that ongoing work is preserved.

This change does not affect the Debezium code, versioning, or release cadence. It is a process change that brings our issue tracking closer to where contributions already happen.

Migration timeline

To minimize disruption, the migration from Jira to GitHub will happen in stages:

  • December 11th, 2025 – Automatic migration of open Jira issues to GitHub Issues.

  • December 11th – 19th, 2025 – Transition period in which the team will manually move any new Jira issues to GitHub.

  • After December 19th, 2025 – Jira is switched to read-only mode; GitHub Issues becomes the sole system of record.

During the transition window, the Debezium team will actively monitor both Jira and GitHub to make sure that any newly created Jira issues are captured and migrated.

How existing Jira issues will be migrated

To keep the process simple and predictable, we will migrate only the most important parts of each open Jira issue:

  • The issue title will become the GitHub issue title.

  • The issue description will become the GitHub issue body.

  • The component(s) will become the GitHub issue label(s).

  • The Fix version will become the GitHub Project iteration.

Additional Jira metadata such as status, resolution, most of labels and custom fields will not be copied automatically. In practice, this means that:

  • The Debezium team will triage migrated issues in GitHub and add appropriate labels and milestones if necessary.

  • Any follow-up details or clarifications can be added directly as comments on the GitHub issue.

To keep the history of each issue connected across systems, we will:

  • Add a comment to the original Jira issue with a link to the corresponding GitHub issue.

  • Add a comment to the GitHub issue that links back to the original Jira ticket.

This way, you can always navigate between the original Jira context and the new GitHub issue if you need to reference older discussion or attachments.

What you need to do as a user or contributor

For most users, no immediate action is required. However, depending on how you interact with Debezium today, you might want to use GitHub Issues for new reports.

Starting December 11th, 2025, we ask you to fill any new bugs or feature requests directly in GitHub Issues instead of Jira. If necessary please update your documentation and internal links.

If you maintain internal documentation, or wiki pages that point to Jira tickets, you might want to update those references over time to use the new GitHub issues.

If you previously relied on Jira notifications, consider watching the relevant Debezium repositories on GitHub to stay informed about new issues and discussions.

What happens to closed Jira issues?

Closed Jira issues will remain in Jira as historical records. They will not be migrated to GitHub.

You will still be able to browse closed tickets and use them as references while Jira remains accessible in read-only mode. Over time, more and more of the "living" history of Debezium will naturally move to GitHub through new issues and pull requests.

Why this change now?

Moving Debezium to the Commonhaus Foundation gives us an opportunity to revisit some of our long-standing processes and align them with a broader, foundation-driven governance model.

Consolidating issue tracking on GitHub helps us to:

  • Reduce friction for new contributors who are already familiar with GitHub.

  • Keep issues, discussions, and pull requests in a single place.

  • Take advantage of GitHub-native workflows, such as project boards, automation, and cross-repository tracking.

Ultimately, this change should make it easier for you to:

  • Report bugs and ask for new features.

  • Follow the progress of issues that matter to you.

  • Collaborate with the Debezium team and the broader community.

A note of thanks to Red Hat

Before we close, we would also like to express our sincere thanks to Red Hat for hosting the Debezium Jira project for many years. It has been an essential part of how we collaborated with users, tracked bugs, and planned new features. We truly appreciate this long-standing support, which helped Debezium grow from a small experiment into a vibrant open source project.

Looking ahead

The move from Jira to GitHub Issues is one of several steps in Debezium’s transition to the Commonhaus Foundation. As we progress, we will continue to refine our contribution guidelines, governance, and tooling to better support a diverse and growing community.

We appreciate your patience during this transition and welcome your feedback. If you have questions about the migration or run into any problems with issues that were moved from Jira, please let us know through our usual channels:

  • Zulip chat

  • The Debezium Debezium mailing list

On behalf of the Debezium team, thank you for being part of this journey with us. We are excited about what this new chapter at Commonhaus will enable—and we look forward to building it together with you.

item.title: CQRS Design Pattern
item.dc:creator: Vojtěch Juránek
item.description:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is a design pattern that separates read and write operations to and from the database. It can also be used to aggregate data from multiple sources into a single, centralized data store. Although this pattern is commonly used in microservice architectures, it is not limited to them. In this blog post, we will explore how to implement the pattern in different setups and how Debezium can simplify its implementation.

This is one of the most common questions from our community.

If you ask The Ultimate Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, the answer to everything is 42. Sadly, in the real world, it’s not quite that simple. The real answer is: it depends.

With this article, I’d like not only to provide an answer by walking through different scenarios, but also to explain the reasons behind it.
